response.text:
In mid-sixteenth-century London, two boys are born on the same autumn day: Tom Canty in the squalor of Offal Court to a brutal father, and Edward Tudor in regal splendor to the adoring nation as Prince of Wales. Tom grows up under the blows of John Canty and the benevolent tutelage of a displaced priest, filling his head with stories of kings until he longs to see one. That dream comes true when he wanders to Westminster and is beckoned inside by the curious, generous Edward, who is fascinated by Tom’s life among commoners. On a whim, the boys trade clothes and marvel at their identical looks, but the jest turns dire when a sentry ejects the ragged “pauper”—the real prince—into the streets, while Tom is trapped inside as courtiers mistake him for their sovereign. Henry VIII is near death, and the court smothers scandal by calling Tom’s bewilderment a passing malady, schooling him to nod and reign while Lord Hertford and Sir John guide him through audiences, banquets, and the ever-ominous question of the missing Great Seal. Outside, the dispossessed Edward is jeered as a lunatic, seized by John Canty, and plunged into a world of want, where the trappings of royalty bring no shelter.

Edward’s bitter education continues among beggars, thieves, and cruel laws: he is dragged by Canty’s gang, briefly sheltered by a fanatical hermit who nearly kills him, and finally rescued by the down-at-heel but gallant soldier Miles Hendon. Miles, convinced his “mad” foundling is harmless, takes him under his protection and dreams of recovering his own usurped inheritance from his treacherous brother, Hugh, and beloved Edith. The prince and the veteran tramp the country, share hunger and cold, and repeatedly see the iron teeth of Tudor justice bite the poor—women burned as witches or heretics, a child doomed for a petty theft, and a man branded and sold for killing a deer. Edward’s outrage hardens into a vow to be a merciful king, even as he is powerless to stop a mother and daughter at the stake and a public scourging in the jail yard. Meanwhile, Tom gradually learns courtly rituals, grows fond of Elizabeth and Jane Grey, softens sentences, and wins the people with his naïve kindness, even dazzling London in a glittering recognition procession. But when his true mother breaks through the crowd to kiss him, shame scorches him—he denies her with a conditioned gesture, then burns with remorse as she is thrust away.

Miles’s own fortunes reverse when he reaches Hendon Hall, only to be repudiated by Edith under Hugh’s threats and flung into jail on false charges. Loyal to the boy who claims to be king, he endures the stocks in Edward’s stead; the watching crowd, impressed by his courage, falls silent as the child secretly dubs him “Earl.” On the eve of the coronation, London is all pageantry: Tom, bemused but dutiful, rides through torrents of applause, then approaches the Abbey while Edward, ragged and hungry, fights his way across the bridge and slips into Westminster among workmen. As the Archbishop of Canterbury lifts the crown and a thousand coronets poise in the air, the true prince strides up the nave and forbids the crowning, while Tom, with sudden relief and gratitude, proclaims him the rightful sovereign. Skeptical lords test the ragged boy with questions only a prince could answer, and doubt gathers—until Tom prompts Edward to recall where he hid the Great Seal on the day of their exchange: in a secret nook of a Milanese arm-piece in the palace. When St. John returns with the gleaming disk, the nave erupts; Tom kneels, Edward is crowned, and the perilous riddle dissolves in thunderous acclaim.

Restorations and reckonings follow swiftly. Miles is publicly honoured for saving the prince from shame and danger, knighted, made Earl of Kent, and granted the singular right for his line to sit in the king’s presence; Hugh is stripped of his thefts and slinks abroad to die, and in time Edith weds Miles after her coerced vows are broken. Tom, tenderly relieved of his heavy masquerade, becomes the King’s Ward and a governor of Christ’s Hospital, distinguished forever by a unique dress that reminds the nation he once bore the weight of a crown. Edward searches out those maimed by injustice: he frees an old lawyer, reclaims a branded farmer from outlawry, rescues condemned children and poor women where he can, and softens the harshest statutes—though sometimes too late, as when a poacher he wishes to save is already hanged. The justice who pitied the “thief of a pig” rises to dignity with the king’s favour; the false friends and brutal officers who scourged the innocent feel the young monarch’s rebukes. Through it all, Edward retells his strange adventure to keep pity sharp in his heart, determined that the sovereign should learn from the subject’s sufferings.

The tale closes with fortunes settled and themes laid bare. Identity proves fragile, subject to the costume on one’s back and the gaze of the crowd, yet character—Tom’s kindness, Edward’s resolve, Miles’s loyalty—shines through disguise. Power, glimpsed from both the marble corridors and the muddy alleys, appears as both spectacle and burden, its true nobility measured by mercy rather than ceremony. Tom lives to honoured old age, saluted in the streets as the King’s Ward; the Kents keep their quaint privilege until it dies on a Civil War battlefield; and Edward VI, reigning briefly, tempers his era’s cruelty with a boy’s conscience. Thus a prince learns humanity among paupers, a pauper learns dignity among princes, and England is better for the exchange.
